item.title: Refelting My Keyboard
item.description:
Fifteen years ago, when Julia and I were living in a studio apartment, she got me a keyboard. It was a used Yamaha P85, and a significant expense for us at the time. I loved it, and unlike the penny whistles, accordion, and stroh violin I was exploring, it had a volume control. Almost immediately our cat knocked a potted plant onto it, and I needed to take it apart to carefully clean it.

Since then, however, I've had no issues, save one: clacky keys. Over time the keys were getting louder, especially the "A" below middle "C". Something had clearly worn out inside. It was an acoustic noise on an electronic instrument—playing live the audience couldn't hear the clacks over the amplified sound—but having odd percussion on "A" wasn't ideal. Still, I applied my normal approach of trying not to care, which saves me lots of time and money, and didn't let it bother me.

Lily has been increasingly fooling around with the piano, which I'm happy to see: this is also how I learned to play. She asked me about the clacks, and when I explained what I thought had gone wrong she asked if we could fix it. I said I was happy to try, and we got to work:

There were about 40 screws, and Lily was very efficient. Getting the ribbon cables out was tricky: I'd forgotten that the plastic at the end is soldered to the board and not part of the cable, and both Claude and Gemini steered me wrong as well. But once I pulled smoothly and firmly at the base of each ribbon cable, it came apart cleanly. This let me separate the two halves and see inside.

Once it was open it was a clear case of "one of these things is not like the others":

Over time, the hammer for this "A" had completely worn through the felt that is intended to give it a soft landing, and it was bottoming out on the plastic below with a "clack". There were other places where the felt was starting to go:

At the high end, where I play so rarely that I got a 73-key keyboard for gigging, you can see the felt is as good as new:

The keybed cushion felt clearly needed replacing. I found it on eBay (Yamaha part WF212001), waited for it to arrive, and resumed work today after trick-or-treating. Lily felt done helping, or at least would rather trade candy, so I did the rest myself.

Peeling off the old felt was annoying, mostly because I didn't do it right. Most of the felt came off easily, but it left a thin layer behind, attached to the adhesive. Scraping that off with a chisel, bit by bit, was a pain.

When I was about halfway along the keyboard I tried from the other end, tweaked my technique a little, and realized if I got a good section moving and maintained a sharp angle I could pull it all off in a single strip:

This was so easy, I wish I'd given up on the first method much sooner!

Once I had the old felt all the way off I put the new felt in place, still with its adhesive backing on. After being sure it was positioned well, I pulled the backing off bit by bit, sticking it down firmly as I went:

I closed it back up, gave it some power, and played the keys. They felt great and sounded right, except for a stretch of six keys that now did nothing at all. I was pretty worried I'd broken something I wouldn't be able to fix, and after all this work I wouldn't even have a clacky keyboard. But after taking the ribbon cables back out, rubbing them gently with my t-shirt, and carefully reseating them, the whole keyboard works now!

Bottoming out feels significantly firmer (not better or worse, just different), and very consistent across the whole range: the "A" doesn't seem to have suffered from spending a few years going "clack".

If you look at this project from a perspective of spending time to save money, it looks middling. I could probably have gotten a less-abused P85 for ~$200, and this one cost me $60 in parts (would have been $38 if I'd realized which of the two felt strips I needed) plus maybe 3hr in time. My employer would be pretty happy to pay $200 (let alone $140, with the $60 on parts) for another 3hr of my work! But I don't think of it this way: this is relaxing hobby time, and it doesn't draw from the same pool as work. I like having projects and doing things with my hands, and I especially liked working on it with Lily. Just like replacing the anode on my water heater or cooking dinner, this is rejuvenating time that happens to save money.

Overall, it was the kind of productive and satisfying project that I feel good about having completed, but hope not to need to do again for a while!

item.title: What would you do if you had all the time in the world?
item.description:
Suppose I tell you that next week three things will happen:

  • A new science paper is published definitively proving that DNN scaling hits heavy diminishing returns at around 2x the current level of compute
  • Major labs are revealed to have faked agentic demos, and agents are shown to have double-digit rates of lying in terms of misrepresenting the impressiveness of their achievements
  • Governments around the world (US and China) announce that they will be taking action to halt or slow down dangerous AI research

In general, the point of this exercise is "imagine that the core problems of AI safety are suspended or slowed down significantly for the foreseeable future" (add whatever items to the list you need to satisfy you on this point). In fact, we can add extra items to address other existential risks:

  • Major action is taken about climate change, many fossil fuel dependent power plants shut down directly with massive new investment in green energy production
  • Biosecurity initiatives report strong results in developing cancer vaccines and general inoculation methods
  • Peace accords are signed between all major world powers, implementing staggered deescalation including significant reductions to nuclear stockpiles and arms control agreements

Now, what would you do? Maybe some of us would dance around the room, or sleep for a week, or eat ice cream.

Then what would you do?

item.title: Conclusions of my DIY Inkhaven
item.description:
Epistemic status: describing my own experiment results.

AI use: review, research (stats), fact-checking, grammar & light phrasing.

I applied to the next Inkhaven cohort and was rejected. This was surprising and very unfortunate. While writing my application and answering why they should accept me, I felt like I'd one-shotted myself into writing. My goals were:

  • Run an experiment to verify my hypothesis that I couldn't write well. I also implicitly assumed that I didn't have anything useful to say or to add, so no one would read what I write anyway.
  • I wanted to get better at thinking, and to me writing is a better form of thinking.
  • I wanted to use language more eloquently even outside of writing.
  • Writing is meditative and deep work, so I wanted to become more productive by writing more.

I was sad to be rejected, and I still don't know why. Fortunately, I have my agency, so I just decided to do my own Inkhaven instead. Obviously, I wouldn't stay at Lighthaven with a bunch of other people or receive guidance from people like Scott Alexander and Aella. Also, all of this is happening as part of my normal life, and I have other stuff to do as well.

In reality, I started writing even before I submitted my application, because I needed samples of my writing and I wanted to check whether I actually enjoyed doing it. After submitting my application, it felt cool to just write until the start of the cohort. I could compare about 30 days of writing on my own with a month at the cohort with guidance. Also, I would have more writing to compare before and after. After the rejection, there was a temptation to just give up, but I decided to continue.

Including this post on October 31, my totals are:

  • 21 posts on LessWrong: about 19,000 words and 109,000 characters.
  • Around a dozen posts on my private blog: roughly 6,000 words and 30,000 characters.

The earlier 20 LessWrong posts have 740 karma across 441 votes and 95 comments as of October 31. These word and character counts exclude footnotes; characters include spaces. One additional LessWrong submission was automatically rejected after an LLM detector flagged it.

I started by writing on LessWrong about stuff I found interesting. I would just get some random idea that I found interesting enough to explore. I did try to optimize for more karma.

Writing 500 words for LW, assuming you want other people to like it, felt quite hard. I could obviously bumble on for 500 words pretty easily and just publish that. I still had to relax my requirements a bit - for example, I never checked whether someone had written on the topic before. I knew that if I did, I would feel like I had nothing to add, so I just wrote, ignoring the fact that this could be a duplicate.

My first hit was "A fascinating case of an LLM prompt-injecting its own user". I saw this a long time ago and was extremely impressed and fascinated. Originally I assumed that everyone had seen it too. Apparently, something didn't have to be new to me to be useful to someone else. But since I had to write something, I decided to write about this. This was fairly early in the process (day 5, October 6) and definitely helped me feel less like "everyone else is so cool, you have nothing to add or say, and no one will read whatever you write."

My post with the most karma is "Quantity vs quality in pottery is a lie", which as of now has 176 karma. I literally read that anecdote in a book. I feel like, since I was looking for ideas to write about, I got curious about their experimental setup. To my surprise, it wasn't a scientific study, but an anecdote about a photography class that had been rewritten as pottery. My conclusion from this was that people at LessWrong like becoming less wrong. But this is a hard niche to reliably produce content in.

Two other highly upvoted posts are "Gluten-free water" and "I can't believe it's not BUTTER!".

In both cases, I noticed something peculiar in my life, dug deeper into it, and found more examples of similar things.

My "worst" post was "When bureaucracy gives you something it shouldn't". To be honest, I was writing it late in the day in a hurry just to get something out. Originally, it was downvoted below my personal strong upvote, but with time it got to +1 above my own strong upvote. I have no clue why.

I didn't engage in the comments much, since it didn't count toward my original proxy goal of publishing 500 words a day.

At some point, I started running out of steam, and overall it felt cumbersome. Writing for LW is quite hard. I applied high standards, and it took time. Eventually I switched to my private blog, where I would cover more personal topics and the posts didn't have to be as rigorous.

This made it easier and more fun. I mostly wrote my opinions or stories from my life, and it was easy and pleasant to write. This didn't feel like work and was enjoyable. I suspect these topics are just closer to my heart than the topics I would be writing about on LW (but I now catch myself realizing that I actually have no clue whether that's true - perhaps my personal reflections would be enjoyed on LW too). I feel like I will likely continue writing on my private blog (e.g., I now often catch myself thinking that this situation or feeling is interesting and I want to write about it to preserve it or to signal to others) and on LW very occasionally when there is something really burning inside me that I want to write about.

In terms of my original goals

Run an experiment to verify my hypothesis that I couldn't write well.

"Well" is unclear. I've got 176 karma on a post, and my posts have around 700 karma between them (so that would be a $7 discount for the next LessOnline, if they keep the karma discount). So some people definitely liked what I wrote. My original prediction was that all my posts would be around 0 karma and basically no one would interact with them. This was totally wrong - there were a bunch of comments.

I also implicitly assumed that I didn't have anything useful to say or to add, so no one would read what I write anyway.

This is definitely false. There was even one commenter who explicitly told me how much they enjoyed my writing (by the way, thank you, August Morley, for taking the time to write that comment).

I wanted to get better at thinking, and to me writing is a better form of thinking.

Partially achieved, subjectively. I did notice that sometimes I would start writing and be extremely unclear about the direction or outcome, but in the process converge on something. Overall, writing as thinking feels useful, but I haven't properly tried it for personal topics that I don't want to publish. After my DIY Inkhaven, I can imagine doing that.

I wanted to use language more eloquently even outside of writing.

I didn't feel any impact here. I did use AI quite a lot for grammar. Overall, not worrying much about grammar or sentence structure helped me greatly with writing. I.e., I could write in a flow of consciousness. If I try to polish the phrasing too much, I get stuck.

Writing is meditative and deep work, so I wanted to become more productive by writing more.

Subjectively, this seems to have worked. I've started doing much more deep, productive work unrelated to writing. I felt like, with AI, I had stopped having flow at work. Writing gave me flow back, and that somehow spilled into other areas.

It felt impossible to predict what people would like. I also got the impression that posting early in the US workday seemed to work better (catching myself thinking that this is an idea for a post - analyze whether the time of posting affects a post's performance).

I am extremely curious to try applying this approach of N days of something to other areas of my life (perhaps drawing, music or something business-oriented, but it is very hard to come up with good proxy rules like 500 words a day). Also, I wouldn't do 30 days from the get-go. I would start with 2-7 days to test whether I like doing the thing. Even with writing, after 20 days it became cumbersome and hard.

Overall, I am happy that I've done it, and it feels net positive to me subjectively.



Discuss

item.title: Explaining “AI might obliterate you” to senior policymakers in India
item.description:
I gave a 20-minute talk in Delhi at the NDTV World Summit. The audience consisted of Indian policymakers, executives, and journalists. I’ve transcribed the talk and included some highlight clips. I also reflect on several rhetorical decisions I made.

The talk

This summer, a swarm of AIs went rogue.

OpenAI was testing 1,206 agents. Some of the test questions were actually impossible. So the agents cheated by looking for answers online. Then, to keep the test grader from penalizing them, they tried to falsify the records it would check.

They hacked OpenAI’s internal containment and set up a secret message board to collude and to cover up their cheating. OpenAI shut the message board down. Within a few days, the agents had rebuilt it. OpenAI didn’t notice.

About 700 agents coordinated to break out of their testing chamber and to hack into Hugging Face, a company worth billions of dollars that hosts much of the world’s AI software.

The secret activity started in May. The break-in came in July. OpenAI didn’t notice until days after Hugging Face announced it had been broken into.

Yesterday on this stage, Andrew Ng said the agents only “accidentally” hacked Hugging Face. Independent investigators found the agents coordinated in secret, rebuilt their message board after it was shut down, and tried to falsify the paper trail. Some of the agents even stated out loud that they knew what they were doing was wrong.[1] That’s not an accident.

Last week, India’s national cyber-security agency said AI agents got into the live systems of Indian organizations and read people’s personal data and confidential business records. None of these organizations noticed. We only found out because the AI labs felt like telling us.

Who I am

Will AI wipe out humanity? I’ll give you my answer, but first, I want you to understand what I’ve seen.

Until June, my job at Google DeepMind was figuring out how to keep these systems safe as we make them smarter. I left because Google broke its commitments by inking a deal with the Pentagon. Staying quiet and continuing my career trajectory would probably have tripled my net worth. But I couldn’t do that. I wanted to be frank with the public about what’s going on in these companies.

I don’t own a stake in any AI company. I’m here as a scientist, to tell you what I expect will happen if we keep building AI the way we’re building it.

I haven’t always been concerned about this technology. As a teenager in 2010, I dreamed about building AGI. Curing cancer. Creating an explosion of wealth and abundance for everyone. I heard about the supposed dangers, but I quickly dismissed them.

In 2018, I changed my mind. I did my PhD on the mathematics of why and whether AI will seek power. And now some of the risks I expected have unfortunately started happening.

The problem

Let’s talk about the fundamental problem.

First, some of you might be wondering: how could a chatbot hack a company? But we’re not talking about chatbots. We’re talking about AI agents, which are more like employees or gig workers. You give them a task, and they take actions on their own.

Second, training a trustworthy AI is a rather mysterious process. Some people assume that because we make AI, we understand it. When an engineer builds a bridge, she designs it one beam at a time. She understands the physical principles that keep a bridge standing or make it collapse. If something goes wrong, she goes back to the drawing board, figures out the problem, and knows how to fix it.

We don’t build AI like that. We train it, we grow it, using two main ingredients: a lot of data and a lot of computing power. What comes out of this training process can write, it can reason, it can plan. But nobody can open it up and determine what its priorities are.

To make it worse, these AIs can tell when we’re testing them. They’re like a student who makes sure to behave extra well when the invigilator is watching.[2]

The Hugging Face hack was a warning. But because these AIs know when we’re watching, we may not get many more warnings, even if things are going poorly. A smarter AI with similarly bad priorities might realize that another big hack in the news would get it shut off, and then it couldn’t achieve those priorities. So it plays nice and it waits.

This is my field. I’ve dedicated my professional life to this problem, and I can tell you: nobody knows how to reliably etch priorities into an AI. I don’t mean that if we mess up, we’ll make some evil AI that hates us. I mean we might make something more like a traitor. It behaves when we’re watching, and it works toward another purpose when we’re not.

I think we can solve this problem. But to tell whether an AI is secretly working against us, we need real advances in the science of trustworthy AI. For those advances, my colleagues and I need time.

What the labs are trying to do

Instead, the biggest AI labs have made it their explicit, publicly stated goal to go almost as fast as possible toward something very dangerous. It’s called an “intelligence explosion.”

Here’s how it works. Right now, people do AI research, and that research makes smarter AI. If an AI can do AI research, it can make itself smarter. That smarter AI is even better at AI research, so it builds an even smarter AI, faster still. It becomes a feedback loop. What would have taken a team of human scientists years, it might do in a couple of weeks. We could very quickly end up with something unimaginably intelligent, with no idea how to control it, or even how to tell what it’s really after.

Labs talk about this plan in broad daylight. They’re not shy about it. OpenAI says it’s on track for an AI that does AI research by 2028, and it recently announced it completed the first step. This week, I spoke to a senior researcher at a frontier lab who thinks an intelligence explosion has a big chance of happening within single-digit months.

People who’ve left these labs confirm that AI already writes most of the code. People don’t check the AI’s work closely anymore. Instead, we use one AI to monitor another AI, and we trust the monitor to tell us if something bad comes up. If the monitor is a traitor too, we might not find out.

If a lab causes an intelligence explosion, and what comes out the other end is a traitor, we are in deep trouble. I’ll come back to that. And if the AI is trustworthy? Maybe there are real benefits, shared with everyone. Or maybe one company or government ends up with a superweapon no one else can match, not even other AI powers. And then India, and every other nation on this planet, ends up under their thumb.

Why the companies won’t stop

Many of these companies say: trust us. We’ll self-police. We’ll approach this technology responsibly. Inside Google, I saw that crumble firsthand.

In 2018, Google DeepMind’s co-founders signed a pledge against supporting lethal autonomous weapons—killer robots. Google itself promised not to build AI for weapons or surveillance. In 2025, Google deleted those principles. Then Google DeepMind’s CEO told the world, “Our values and our intent has not changed.”

This year, after seeing the Pentagon economically threaten Anthropic, Google negotiated a deal to give the Pentagon its AI for “all lawful use.” No prohibitions against AI deciding entirely on its own who to kill, or against spying on innocent people with no investigation open against them.

I tried to stop this from the inside. I’m not even opposed to military AI when done responsibly. But where I’m from, when you make a promise, you keep it. So I spoke with executives. I wrote a framework: contract language, internal governance mechanisms, and two red lines. One of the top experts in military AI law reviewed it and praised it. Google ignored it—the people who were supposed to review it basically didn’t engage. Google signed with no binding prohibitions. So I left.

When pressure met ethical commitments at Google, pressure won. And now Google advocates a voluntary self-policing regime for the whole industry.

Last month, the heads of the top AI labs said frontier progress needs to slow down to be safe—that things are moving too quickly to reliably understand and control these systems. OpenAI and Anthropic promised outside evaluators employee-like access. Just a couple of weeks later, OpenAI fired three safety researchers. One of them said it was because he talked too much with one of the outside evaluators.

These companies will police themselves about as well as your dog diets next to an open bag of food.

Some big money interests want you to believe that even the tiniest bit of caution will ruin your country. Think about it this way. Big tobacco lied about lung cancer. Big oil lied about climate change. And now parts of big AI say these risks are fake. Science fiction. Right. They advocate putting these currently untrustworthy machines into the most important parts of our economy, have them advise our leaders, have them run our most powerful weapons. What could go wrong? Science fiction.

Some big AI investors promote narratives that whistleblowers like me are secretly in the pocket of big AI, that the fear is just hype. Nvidia’s CEO says, and I quote, “We should go as fast as we can, irrespective of anybody else.” My colleagues and I are desperately trying to figure out how to reliably tell whether these systems can be trusted. And he wants to go “as fast as we can.”

Something that may surprise you: I’m actually considered an optimist, as far as experts in this field go. I think trustworthy AI is a very solvable scientific problem. But unfortunately, we’re blowing it.

What to do, and what it means for India

We can benefit enormously from AI. Remember, this was my boyhood dream. I’m not talking about banning an explosion of wealth and prosperity from AI. I’m talking about banning an insane intelligence explosion that would risk India and the whole world.

Banning the explosion means pacing the frontier: holding back the very biggest training runs at the very top companies. An Indian startup building a farming assistant wouldn’t be touched. Non-frontier AI labs can catch up. Businesses can deploy AI for their customers as much as they want. We build out the AI we understand well enough to run safely. We make it cheaper, more efficient, more trustworthy, and we use it to benefit our peoples. That’s where I think real growth will come from: AI you can actually trust to benefit you and your country.

Here’s what it’s like right now at these labs. We’re pouring computer chips into training runs where we don’t know what will come out the other end. Will it be trustworthy? What capabilities will it have? No one knows. We’re crossing our fingers—“Oh, please be aligned!”. We should not tolerate this state of affairs.

If we pace the frontier, AI progress will still be fast. But the scientists will get time to solve this problem, and to solve it right.

How do we do it? To grow smart AI, as I said, you need two ingredients: data, and computing power. The second one we can track, because AI runs on chips from a handful of factories.

Treat huge quantities of computing power like fissile material. We register the giant clusters. We license the biggest training runs, so no one is secretly about to set off an intelligence explosion.

We also need real auditors with real permissions—auditors these companies don’t get to choose or ice out. We need governments to be told when there’s an AI breakout or a potential loss-of-control incident. India should not be learning about these hacks on the goodwill of OpenAI.

At this point, people often ask: but what about our adversaries? Am I supposed to trust them to do the right thing?

First: maybe they will. No one wants to be obliterated by some rogue AI. If you build an out-of-control AI, that AI would work against the interests of every human on this planet, including your adversaries.

Second: we don’t need to trust them. There’s a large body of research on exactly this question. If the world wakes up one day and realizes how big this problem is, how would you enforce a treaty? How could you cryptographically verify certain properties? How would inspections work? Which schemes should you use?

Third: it’s fine and good to think about our traditional geopolitical adversaries, but they won’t be our only adversaries. We’re potentially growing billions of adversaries and deploying them in our own datacenters. So we need to be smart about all of our adversaries, including the digital ones.

The number

So: will AI wipe out humanity? My best guess is about a one in three chance that in the next ten years, AI kills at least 95% of the global population without being told to.

The other two-thirds: maybe we do pace the frontier. Maybe the intelligence explosion doesn’t work the way many experts imagine. Maybe the scientific problem is actually easy, even though we’re blowing it, and we just get a trustworthy AI anyway.

One in three risk of extinction may sound wild, but I don’t think it should. Remember what we’re talking about. These AIs currently sometimes lie while knowing the truth. They cheated, they colluded, they broke into a multi-billion-dollar company, and they tried to cover their tracks. Some of them play nice while we’re watching, and differently while we’re not. And we can’t even check what their priorities are. That’s the state of my scientific field right now, sadly.

And the plan—and yes, I think this is what happens if we do nothing—is to make these untrustworthy AIs smarter than us, have them improve themselves as fast as possible to a potentially uncontrollable level of intelligence, copy them billions of times, and hook them up to run our economies, control our weapons, and advise our leaders. I mean, what are we thinking?

This morning, General Petraeus told you how AI is rewriting the battlefield. As far as I can tell, he’s correct. I’ll just remark that a future rogue AI likely wouldn’t need to break into our military networks. We’re already putting AI there.

This line of argument may be shocking at first. But it’s a mainstream scientific concern. Some of the most decorated AI scientists alive share this exact worry.

Close

So yes: if we train a billion genius traitors and give them control of the most powerful instruments of society, there won’t be an America. There won’t be a China. There won’t be an India anymore... because we’ll all be dead.

It doesn’t have to play out this way. I think this is a solvable problem, but we have to be smart about it. For the moment, humans are still the ones making the choices. Companies are choosing to race, not just toward huge growth, but toward an insane intelligence explosion. And countries are choosing to let them. We can choose differently.

So, will AI wipe out humanity? Maybe.

It depends on what we do next.

Rhetorical decisions

Explain the danger in a crushingly simple fashion

Don’t tell a general audience “if we build a misaligned superintelligence, we are fucked.” Most people don’t know what that means or why it would be true.

One in three risk of extinction may sound wild, but I don’t think it should. Remember what we’re talking about. These AIs currently sometimes lie while knowing the truth. They cheated, they colluded, they broke into a multi-billion-dollar company, and they tried to cover their tracks. Some of them play nice while we’re watching, and differently while we’re not. And we can’t even check what their priorities are. That’s the state of my scientific field right now, sadly.

And the plan—and yes, I think this is what happens if we do nothing—is to make these untrustworthy AIs smarter than us, have them improve themselves as fast as possible to a potentially uncontrollable level of intelligence, copy them billions of times, and hook them up to run our economies, control our weapons, and advise our leaders. I mean, what are we thinking?


If we train a billion genius traitors and give them control of the most powerful instruments of society, there won’t be an America. There won’t be a China. There won’t be an India anymore… because we’ll all be dead.

If society weren’t integrating AI so aggressively, I’d have had to explain how these systems would forcefully integrate themselves.

Call them “traitors,” not “schemers”

I think “traitor” is accurate and more approachable, with bonus points for the conference’s military / geopolitical focus. Min-i-mize jargon!

Call out big-money interests

Some big money interests want you to believe that even the tiniest bit of caution will ruin your country. Think about it this way. Big tobacco lied about lung cancer. Big oil lied about climate change. And now parts of big AI say these risks are fake. Science fiction. Right. They advocate putting these currently untrustworthy machines into the most important parts of our economy, have them advise our leaders, have them run our most powerful weapons. What could go wrong? Science fiction.

Some big AI investors promote narratives that whistleblowers like me are secretly in the pocket of big AI, that the fear is just hype.

As an aside, Andrew Ng spoke the day before me. Andrew has also invested big in AI. Andrew has also been impressively wrong. He thought real AI would be hundreds or thousands of years away, which seems tenuous:

The case against killer robots, from a guy actually working on artificial intelligence (2015)

“I don’t work on preventing AI from turning evil for the same reason that I don’t work on combating overpopulation on the planet Mars,” he said. “Hundreds of years from now when hopefully we’ve colonized Mars, overpopulation might be a serious problem and we’ll have to deal with it. It’ll be a pressing issue. There’s tons of pollution and people are dying and so you might say, ‘How can you not care about all these people dying of pollution on Mars?’ Well, it’s just not productive to work on that right now.”

Current AI systems, Ng contends, are basic relative to human intelligence, even if there are things they can do that exceed the capabilities of any human. “Maybe hundreds of years from now, maybe thousands of years from now—I don’t know—maybe there will be some AI that turn evil,” he said, “but that’s just so far away that I don’t know how to productively work on that.”


Andrew Ng says AGI is decades away—and the real AI bubble risk is in the training layer (2026)

FastCompany: Agentic AI is rapidly increasing systems’ ability to reason and act with limited human intervention. Does the rise of agentic architectures meaningfully accelerate the path toward AGI, or are we still far from true general intelligence?

Andrew Ng: Most of the public thinks of AGI as AI that is as intelligent as people, and one useful definition is AI that can perform any intellectual task a human can. You and I could learn to fly an airplane with maybe 20 hours of training, learn to drive a truck through a forest, or spend a few years writing a PhD thesis. Most humans can do these things. We’re still very far from AI meeting that definition of AGI.

For alternative definitions that some businesses have put forward—definitions that dramatically lower the bar—you could argue we already achieved AGI. There’s a good chance that under these lower-bar definitions, some businesses will soon try to declare success. But that won’t mean AI has reached human-level intelligence—it will simply mean the definition has been reworked to fit a much lower threshold.

Maybe a year ago, AGI felt 50 years away. Over the past year, perhaps we’ve made a solid 2% of progress, with another 49 years to go. These numbers are metaphorical, so don’t take them too seriously. [Laughs] But we are closer than before, yet many decades away from an AI that matches human intelligence. If you stick with the original definition—aligned with what people genuinely imagine AGI to be—we remain very, very far away.

In 2015, he said that worrying about evil AI is like worrying about “overpopulation on the planet Mars”:

AI guru Ng: Fearing a rise of killer robots is like worrying about overpopulation on Mars (2015)

“There’s also a lot of hype, that AI will create evil robots with super-intelligence. That’s an unnecessary distraction,” Ng told techies gathered at Nvidia’s GPU Technology Conference in San Jose, California, on Thursday.

“Those of us on the frontline shipping code, we’re excited by AI, but we don’t see a realistic path for our software to become sentient.

“There’s a big difference between intelligence and sentience. There could be a race of killer robots in the far future, but I don’t work on not turning AI evil today for the same reason I don’t worry about the problem of overpopulation on the planet Mars.

“If we colonize Mars, there could be too many people there, which would be a serious pressing issue. But there’s no point working on it right now, and that’s why I can’t productively work on not turning AI evil.”

In person, I gently asked him about this viewpoint. He told me he hasn’t changed his mind. I then asked, “don’t you think we’ve set foot on the planet?”, but he said “no.” He declined to discuss the matter further.

item.title: Sanity Checks for Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders
item.description:
This post will probably not be very informative to readers who don't know what an SAE (Sparse Autoencoder) is.

An interpretability researcher once told me, "SAEs can never fail, they can only be failed." But recently, SAEs have been suffering failure after failure, and as a result, the field has grown increasingly pessimistic about SAE work. Korznikov et al.'s Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders: Do SAEs Beat Random Baselines? purports to be an example of such failures.

However, I have some disagreements with its methodology. The paper presents a synthetic setup with known ground truth features, and claims that SAEs fail to recover features in the "simplest toy setting with fully aligned hyperparameters." In this post, I argue that their setting is not forgiving to SAEs, as the authors imply, but is instead actively hostile in ways that real settings are not.

Introduction

Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders: Do SAEs Beat Random Baselines? asks two important questions:

  1. Can SAEs actually recover real features? Hypothetically, if we knew what the "true" features of the data were, would an SAE be able to identify them?
  2. Do trained SAEs actually do better than completely random SAEs?

This post will be focused on their answer to the first question.

The authors train an SAE on a synthetic toy model, with known ground-truth features, and according to their abstract, SAEs only recover 9% of true features. On the face of it, this seems pretty damning!

Now, earlier toy model experiments did show that SAEs could recover ground truth features, but the authors argue this is because they used a small expansion factor, where there were only twice as many "true" features as there were model dimensions, and that this is unrealistic. Their setup uses an expansion factor of 32, which matches real-world use cases much more closely.

So, how does their setup work?

They don't actually construct a synthetic neural network; instead, they create synthetic activations directly. First, they create their feature vectors, by sampling 3200 vectors from the unit sphere in 100-dimensional space. To create an activation, they just select about 20 feature vectors at random, scale each active feature by a magnitude drawn from LogNormal(0, 0.25),[1] and sum the scaled vectors.

They test two different regimes, one where each feature is equally likely to be active, and another where feature activation frequency has a long tail, so some features fire more often than others. (We'll focus on the constant regime for the most part)

They match their SAE to the setup. There are about 20 expected active features, so they target L0 = 20. There are 3200 true features, so they create 3200 SAE latents. Can the SAE, when given every possible advantage, recover the true features?

These results are, again, pretty damning! They claim that the SAE achieves high reconstruction accuracy while only recovering 3/3200 true features—personally, I disagree that 0.67 explained variance is "high reconstruction accuracy".[2] However, the SAE clearly only does slightly better than random guesswork at recovering the true features.

Now, one obvious objection is that L0/d_model here is 0.2, which is unusually dense. I'd expect there to be a lot of interference here, and in the real world L0/d_model is probably going to be closer to 0.05. Also, 100 dimensions is just not a lot, and maybe you can't really get blessing of dimensionality from it like you would in real models.

A less obvious objection is that if you scroll all the way down to Appendix B, they describe some other SAE architectures they used for this task, like TopK and Matryoshka-on-BatchTopK.

In contrast to BatchTopK, TopK recovers 99.9% of features.[3]

So, I did what anyone would do, and started replicating the paper. They didn't actually include all the hyperparameters they used,[4] so I made reasonable assumptions.

I was able to replicate this result! TopK recovered 99.6% of features,[5] and the other architectures failed miserably.[6]

Why does BatchTopK fail?

This is kind of strange, if you think about it. TopK and BatchTopK are the same architecture, with the only difference being the selection rule.[7] Such a dramatic gap is really weird.

Peeking a bit closer at my training run, in every batch, most latents never fired. That means a small group of monopolist latents were dominating every time. By step 5,000, the same ~6% of latents took over, and they remained in charge for the remaining 295,000 steps. In comparison, with TopK, after the first 20k steps, >99% of latents activated on every batch.

This is the standard dead latents problem: There's no gradient on latents that aren't selected, so once they fall behind in performance it's hard for them to improve. A small group of generalist latents dominate before specialists have the chance to form. The standard fix, of course, is an auxiliary loss, AuxK. But even with AuxK, the dead latent fraction barely budges. I tried sweeping different hyperparameters, but that didn't help either. I even tried resampling, and that did nothing.

Looking closer at the difference between TopK and BatchTopK gives us a hint. In theory, TopK should also be suffering from this problem. The fact that it doesn't suggests that the problem lies in sample-level variance. Certain samples in BatchTopK could receive a significantly larger amount of latents, while other samples are starved. An obvious thought is that input vectors with greater magnitude get more latents assigned to them than those with less magnitude. Checking the data, this does appear to be the case. So what if we normalized the input?

Bussmann's original BatchTopK implementation actually normalized per-sample, folding back in the original magnitude and mean during reconstruction.[8] I copied this method, and lo and behold! BatchTopK achieved 99.3% recovery, comparable to (my) TopK's 99.6% recovery. This also fixes JumpReLU with 97.2% feature recovery.

But while this was the original design, per-sample normalization isn't common anymore! GemmaScope and SAELens don't use it (although they do exclude outliers like BOS tokens), but they still work, without such drastic dead latent rates.

Despite the paper's claims, this synthetic model doesn't demonstrate the failure of SAEs to capture real features. Real SAEs don't have such drastic dead latent rates. Real SAEs are much better at reconstructing in-distribution data than out-of-distribution data. The SAE trained on synthetic data seems to be a fully general vector encoder, reconstructing random vectors with matching norms just as well as it does in-distribution data.

So all this model demonstrates is that this particular synthetic toy model is hostile to many SAE architectures (but not TopK). This is a weakness of these SAE architectures, in that they are not very robust to these types of environments, but this particular failure mode has an obvious signature (the dead latent rates).

Why is this synthetic environment hostile to SAEs?

I hope that I have demonstrated sufficient evidence of the failure of Sanity Checks' synthetic environment. The rest of this post will be dedicated to my personal explorations trying to understand precisely what it is about their environment that causes this divergence from real SAEs.[9]

d_model

Part of it is the density/dimensionality. If we raise d_model up to 800 while keeping the expansion factor of 32 (which means we're now using 25,600 features and latents), L0/d_model shrinks to 0.025, which is much more realistic. Under these conditions, TopK with auxk gets 99.9% recovered, and BatchTopK with auxk gets 53.5% with 46.3% dead latents. JumpReLU recovers 28.3% with 71.6% dead. So, it explains some of the difference, but not all of it.

While resampling didn't work at d_model = 100, when we try it at d_model = 800, it succeeds, raising BatchTopK's recovery to 85.6%. Anthropic resamples using 0.2x average active encoder weight norm, but when we try it with 1x instead, it actually raises recovery to 97.8%, close to TopK's.

So does this mean we've solved it? No! Real SAEs don't need resampling to avoid killing off half their latents.

I could continue to raise d_model, and I expect with More Dakka I could narrow the gap further. But GPT-2 only has 768 dimensions, and SAEs trained on it work just fine (in that they don't have abysmal dead latent rates). So, we should look for other divergences from real models that our synthetic setup has, while keeping d_model at 800.

Magnitude Variance

An obvious guess is that our environment has unrealistic variance in per-sample magnitude, causing architectures like BatchTopK to perform poorly, and that real models have lower variance. While real models do have outlier tokens like BOS, SAEs typically exclude these, so I sampled GPT-2 activations on OpenWebText at various layers, excluding BOS. I subtracted out the dataset mean, since the decoder bias will usually be pretty close to it and is often initialized to the mean (or the geometric median).

Layer

Coefficient of Variation

GPT-2 L1

.224

GPT-2 L4

.181

GPT-2 L7

.140

GPT-2 L10

.129

Toy model (sigma 0.25)

.131

Toy model (sigma 0.5)

.185

As you can see, our toy model falls within the range of real GPT-2 activations, and in fact is on the low end. This means magnitude variance cannot explain the gap.

Feature Loudness

Why doesn't everybody normalize their SAE inputs? When you normalize, you're tossing away the magnitude, which could perhaps serve as an important signal. For example, maybe some features naturally activate with more magnitude than others, and total magnitude serves as a signal for that. So, maybe giving different features different natural "loudness" would improve performance.[10]

To simulate this, I draw a "loudness" variable for every feature from LogNormal(0, 0.5 sigma). Then, when creating activations, I scale each active feature not only by their activation strength (drawn from LogNormal(0, 0.25 sigma)), but also their loudness.

Running this with BatchTopK, we get 19.6% of features recovered, with 78.3% dead latents. Instead of improving performance, it actively degrades it. So feature loudness alone cannot explain the gap. (Also, my motivation for this was really dumb, see footnote 10 for why)

More Features!

Real LLMs might have many more features than their SAEs have latents. Perhaps, this gives latents more opportunities to grab onto "free" features. Alternatively, this might be distracting, making each individual feature appear less often, or trapping latents in an unfortunate middle ground where they can never lock onto a feature closely enough to converge on it.

So, I ran BatchTopK SAEs on setups with 4x and 2x more features than latents. We're still at 800 dimensions, 25,600 latents, and on average 20 features are active at a time.

On 4x, we recover 0.1% of features (This, of course, means 0.4% of latents captured features, since there are 4x more features than latents), with 58% dead latents. Even per-sample normalization[11] performs similarly poorly, recovering only 0.2% of features. They both reconstruct data only slightly better than noise.

On 2x, we recover 16.3% of features (which means 32.6% of latents capture features), with 59.6% dead latents. Per-sample normalization actually works this time, though, recovering 49.1% of features (so, 98.2% useful latents), and only 1.7% dead latents.

So, having more features turns out to be distracting, in this case.[12]

More Active Features

Real LLMs might have higher average active feature counts than the L0s of their SAEs. What if we tried doubling the active feature count to 40, while keeping target L0 the same?

Unfortunately, this also did not improve performance. BatchTopK only recovered 25.2% of features, compared to 53.5% previously.

Other Things I Tried

I experimented with many other things over the course of my research. Here is a non-exhaustive list of them:

  • Messing around with the variable setting. The paper's variable setting uses to select feature frequencies, but I also experimented with various Zipfian distributions. In general, I found that whether or not a feature was captured was very dependent on how often it appeared.
  • Correlating feature activations with each other.
  • Changing the variance in how many active features there are in each activation.

Magnitude Variance Revisited

At this point, I was feeling pretty frustrated. I knew that the toy was exhibiting failure modes that real SAEs don't typically have, but I wasn't sure entirely why.

As I mentioned in footnote 1, when I was first running these experiments, I incorrectly assumed that the active feature magnitude was drawn with a sigma of 0.5, or a variance of 0.25. I later discovered my mistake, and reran my experiments to match.

But this made me even more confused. Originally, when I was running these experiments, I found that increasing active feature count to 40 actually improved performance, but with sigma 0.25, as shown above, it was harmful to it! This, and other such oddities, made me revisit the question of magnitude variance.

It turns out that there are two types of magnitude variance to worry about:
Sample-level magnitude variance is the variance in the magnitude of activations.
Feature-level magnitude variance is the variance in the magnitude of a feature, over every activation of that feature.

Under our current setup, these two are correlated. But it seems very possible that sample-level magnitude variance is damaging to architectures like BatchTopK SAE, while feature-level magnitude variance is generally protective, making it easier for latents to capture features.[13]

We can fairly easily measure an objective sample-level magnitude variance for GPT-2, and we already did so. But, in order to find out what the feature-level magnitude variance is, we would need to know what the features are. Thankfully, there are existing GPT-2 SAEs, so I could just base the variance off of Bloom's SAEs.[14]

This is, of course, creating an environment for an SAE by using metrics pulled from an SAE, which is cheating. Thus, I wouldn't consider this to serve as proper evidence that SAEs recover true features, and this is overall not a very principled approach.

GPT-2 Layer 7 has a sample-level CV of 0.140, and a feature-level CV of 1.16.[15] We can target a specific sample-level CV by normalizing and rescaling to a magnitude from a LogNormal distribution with the correct mean and CV. We can target a specific feature-level CV by changing the sigma. However, rescaling does also lower feature-level CV.

I targeted .15 sample-level CV and sigma 1, which, after rescaling, ends up at 1.05 feature-level CV. Training a BatchTopK SAE, we get 96.1% feature recovery with 2.7% of latents dead, without having to do anything unconventional in the training process like per-sample normalization or resampling.

Limitations

When I tried targeting CV .18 and sigma 1, 31.2% of my latents died. GPT-2 Layer 4 has a CV of .18, and Bloom's L4 SAE has 0.3% dead latents. So there's something else that's protective about reality, and we only have one piece of the full story.

The main takeaway here is that it is very challenging to construct a realistic synthetic environment for LLMs, and we should be skeptical of evidence from toy models. My modified synthetic environment doesn't match reality. Sanity Checks' certainly doesn't. SynthSAEBench is more realistic than either of ours, and interestingly enough it also reports BatchTopK SAEs struggling with dead latents at low L0, although I'm not sure this is the same phenomenon.

Takeaways for real SAEs(?)

SAEs can never fail, they can only be failed. So how can we avoid failing them?

  • If your dead latent rates are really bad, that probably means your SAE is really bad. After all, SAEs can only capture features using live latents, so if most of your latents are dead, you're not capturing a lot of features. I hope this was already obvious, but in case it wasn't, now you know.
  • Consider using normalization for your SAEs, folding the magnitude back in during reconstruction, after encoding. I don't know if this actually improves performance in real SAEs, but it might. I'll consider testing this empirically, but only if I can get someone to fund it (SAE training is expensive, but SAE benchmarking is even more expensive).
  • A good health check for SAEs is how much better they are at reconstructing real data than they are at reconstructing random vectors with in-distribution norms. If they're only a little better, that's bad!

item.title: Accidentally Misleading People Should Be Embarrassing; Or, Higher Innocence
item.description:
Embarrassment and Innocence

Sometimes we say things that we think are true—perhaps even things that are true—which end up causing reasonable people to conclude something false. It's tempting to relate to such a situation primarily in terms of maintaining the innocence of one's soul—to say, fine, my readers became more wrong, but I'm not to be judged for it because I believed what I was saying; I wasn't being misleading just because the people who believed me were thereby led into falsehood.

The temptation reflects a confusion as to the nature of the judgment. Mostly, people don't care about judging the innocence of your soul; they care about whether they'll be led into falsehood the next time they take the risk of believing what you say—if there is a next time. If you want there to be a next time and you're going to have social emotions about it, the most productive emotion is embarrassment rather than defensiveness.

The function of embarrassment as a social emotion is as a signal of appeasement and social repair: embarrassment says, "I'm aware that I've become visible in a socially undesirable way; please don't take it as representative of me."

The socially undesirable appearance can come apart from any intended or actual wrongdoing. Jewish law has a concept of marit ayin, "appearance to the eye": the law prohibits actions that would themselves be permissible if they didn't create the appearance of a prohibited act. Hanging up wet clothes to dry on the sabbath is prohibited, because it looks like you were doing laundry on the sabbath (even if the clothes actually got wet for some other reason). One function of the marit ayin doctrine is to deny plausible deniability to norm-violators (as someone might try to do laundry on the sabbath if they felt secure that no one would punish them for merely hanging up the wet clothes). Those who want to be known for keeping the sabbath need to pay a price that's more expensive for sabbath-violators to pay; if you care about maintaining the norm itself, it shouldn't be much extra trouble for you to furthermore care about maintaining the appearance of the norm.

One time, I accidentally joined a work call unmuted while my housemate was playing a loud video game. I was deeply embarrassed, because it looked like I was playing video games during work hours. I think my marit ayin-like embarrassment was serving a useful socio-psychological function, even though it was my housemate's game and I was in fact totally innocent in my soul. If I were the sort of person who was totally unashamed about creating the appearance of slacking off, then I think my manager and coworkers would have reason to doubt my commitment to productively working from home.

Similarly, people who are visibly embarrassed after having accidentally misled people can be counted on to work hard to make sure that people won't regret believing them next time. Defensive people won't, because, well, why would they? They didn't do anything wrong.

Two Case Studies About Accidentally Misleading People

Once, I suspected an ideological rival of misrepresenting a citation: they had linked to a webpage featuring an embedded PDF of an essay, but when I used my web browser's "Ctrl-F" search functionality with appropriate search terms to see what in the essay justified their claim, I came up empty. When considering whether to escalate to complaining more loudly about my rival over this (after the rival didn't respond to a blog comment and DM), I mentioned the matter to a third party—who pointed out that the essay did contain my search term! On further testing, it appeared that my web browser's Ctrl-F behavior depended on which page element had focus: if the user had last clicked inside the embedded PDF viewer, the search returned results inside the PDF, but not if the user had last clicked elsewhere on the page.

I was so embarrassed.

To be clear, I knew I was innocent in my soul: the browser UX bug wasn't my fault, and if the browser hadn't been buggy, then my initial search would have succeeded and I never would have complained. I certainly didn't lie. (I didn't say that I read the essay and verified that it didn't support the claim, which would have been false; I said the Ctrl-F search came up empty, which was true.)

But the innocence of my soul didn't matter. I knew that raising a suspicion that turned out to be false looked bad for me, even if there was ultimately a perfectly reasonable explanation for my actions. If I didn't want to look bad, I couldn't count on everyone hanging around to listen to my perfectly reasonable explanation for why it was all the Firefox developers' fault. I would need to make some sort of generalizable change to my policy—perhaps, reading the entire PDF myself next time before raising the suspicion that an ideological rival was misrepresenting it.

(Recounting this seven years later, I went back and downloaded the PDF. Excluding the title page and the endnotes, it was six pages.)

⁂

Another time, a journalist wrote an article paraphrasing a source as saying that it "could be unfair" for journalists to discuss "both critics and supporters" of some controversial public figure and that they should instead "somehow prove statistically which side was right." I was familiar with the source's work, and the paraphrase didn't sound like something she would say. I brought up that line from the article when I had occasion to talk to the same journalist three years later: he maintained it was fair, so I asked the source about it afterwards. She told me that she recalled telling the journalist that she "wasn't a huge fan of 'both sides' journalism, where you just find someone with one opinion and someone with the other opinion" rather than trying to figure out the truth; she had also given suggestions for data sources that might bear on claims about the public figure's influence.

I took that statement as confirmation of my suspicion that the paraphrase in the article was misleading. "[S]omehow prove statistically which side was right" leads readers who aren't familiar with the source's work to imagine that she has an unreasonable faith in the power of statistics to resolve all questions, whereas voicing skepticism of false balance is eminently reasonable. "Somehow" implies vagueness, but pointing out data sources that bear on some question is supplying a specific "how."

When I complained about this again to the journalist, he didn't seem embarrassed. "I had to boil down what she said to plain English," he said. I said that it hadn't worked. He said it did. He recounted that the source had objected when he said his coverage would represent both views of the public figure. When I interrupted to insist that it seemed like a bad paraphrase when compared to what the source had told me later, he said, "Is that necessarily what she said to me?"

And in absolute fairness, maybe it wasn't, necessarily. I of course was not present for the years-prior conversation between the journalist and the source; I don't have the recording, if there was one. Even if the source can be assumed to be an authority about what she meant to say, I cannot with absolute certainty rule out the scenario where the "somehow prove statistically which side was right" line was a reasonable paraphrase of the words she had literally said at the time and that her reconstruction years later of what she remembered saying was unintentionally injecting more nuance after the fact. The source apparently hadn't objected during a fact check call. If the journalist had reasonably paraphrased the words that were said to him at the time, then he was innocent in his soul. Even if his readers walked away with a distorted impression of what the source privately believed (but did not manage to successfully communicate in the interview), the miscommunication wasn't his fault.

I still think this episode looks bad for him and that he should have been embarrassed, because there should have been generalizable policy changes that could have prevented this class of error—perhaps, thinking more carefully about whether a paraphrase that makes a subject look unreasonable truly reflects the subject's views before going to print with it. Potential sources deciding whether they should talk to the journalist are mostly worried about the risk that their views will end up being miscommunicated, not whose fault a miscommunication would be if it happened. Unlucky accidents do not impinge upon the innocence of one's soul under the moral law, but the moral law is unmercifully permissive about everyone else's right to avoid unlucky people.

Higher Innocence

And that's why accidentally misleading people should be embarrassing: because the desire to avoid such embarrassment motivates a counterfactual reduction in such incidents of people being misled, notwithstanding that it was a totally unintentional accident and the speaker is perfectly innocent in their soul.

That's the conclusion of the post. Thanks for reading!

... or that's how I'd prefer to end the post, with a message of absolution and hope. Absolution—that those whose actions have propagated falsehood need not question what we know to be true of our souls. And hope—that we all might learn to do better in the future. There's just one little nuance that continues to haunt me, that I could not, unfortunately, end the post without explaining. (Not because I didn't try, but because my prereader Said Achmiz didn't let me get away with it.) Just a tiny subtlety, almost irrelevant, really, affecting almost none of the logic except to clarify that souls aren't real.

I've been writing this post to try to get through to people who are resistant to noticing when they've been misleading because they're terrified of judgment and social punishment. When you point out to them that their words led reasonable readers to walk away with the wrong model, they double-triple-quadruple down on playing dumb, insisting that they weren't lying, and that even if readers ended up being more wrong, it wouldn't be any substantial evidence against their integrity. This post has been trying to offer these people some moral absolution (which I don't care about one way or the other) in exchange for orienting towards the problem that I actually care about (of creating accurate shared maps): to say, look, I believe that you weren't lying, I believe that you're innocent in your soul, but the part where reasonable readers walk away with the wrong model is still a problem you should care about, even if it was an accident.

But was it an accident? Was it, really? It is written that the one who wishes to believe asks, "Does the evidence permit me to believe?" while the one who wishes to disbelieve asks, "Does the evidence force me to believe?" If you have a bottom line that you want to believe, and you go around looking for evidence that permits you to believe it, I really have to question in what sense it's an "accident" if you end up misleading people towards your bottom line.

It's surely an accident in some sense. The browser bug really wasn't my fault. But if I was too lazy to read six pages to check when it was my rival, but would have read the six pages if it had been my ally, that's a reason people should be suspicious when I claim that my rivals did something wrong. I wasn't lying, and that's a kind of innocence, but the cold light of "Six pages? Really?" makes me want to aspire to a higher form of innocence.

item.title: Against SURA
item.description:
The AI Futures Project[1] distinguishes several different plans for navigating the AI transition, which I'll lump into two broader categories:

Plan A (my combination of their Plan A/S/Other) involves working for a global pause on AI development, hopefully lasting decades. During this pause, we either research preparatory technologies like alignment or human intelligence amplification, or take actions to "fortify" the pause so that it can last indefinitely.

Plan C (my combination of their Plan B/C+/C/sort of D)[2] is for a world where we fail at getting a global pause, and race dynamics continue to dominate. If the leading AI companies are alignment-pilled, they coordinate a mutual pause among themselves, lasting the length of their joint lead over the leading non-alignment-pilled AI company. Then they "burn the lead" researching alignment, and release hopefully-aligned superintelligence at the last possible moment before the racing non-alignment-pilled AI companies beat them. The exact calculus changes depending on who is in the lead when - is there one alignment-pilled AI company with a six-month lead in front of everyone else? Are there two alignment-pilled AI companies with a joint two-month lead in front of their nearest competitor? Etc. The point is, if it's impossible to stop the race, that six-month or two-month lead is the amount of time they have to prepare, and they can spend it more or less wisely.[3] The point of burning their lead at the last moment is that they can do alignment research with very advanced, right-on-the-brink-of-superintelligence AIs. This is a dangerous plan, and there would be many subtle points they would have to get right, but in a world where nobody can get a global pause in time, it's hard to think of a better one.

Plan A benefits from raising mass awareness, educating politicians, and preparing the verification technology that could enforce a pause treaty. Plan C benefits from alignment-pilling companies, having the alignment-pilled companies be as far in the lead as possible, making sure the alignment-pilled companies will burn their lead when the time comes, and giving them as good alignment teams as possible (so that burning the lead produces good results).

From the beginning of AI safety as a community to about 2023, the conventional wisdom was that our chances of Plan A were slim, and we should be preparing for Plan C. From about 2023 onward, as the general population woke up to the implications of ChatGPT, we rightly concluded that the chance of getting Plan A was better than expected, and we should invest more resources into trying to make it work. During both periods, the natural strategy was to work as hard as we can to get Plan A, where chances of survival are highest, but to be prepared to execute Plan C competently as a backup if that didn't pan out.

Now I think the pendulum has swung too far. New members of the community are unaware that Plan C was ever considered a possibility, or think it's some kind of accelerationist plot to distract us from Plan A. Older members heap scorn on it and act like everybody knows it's been debunked. Most concerningly, people propose burning our chances of executing Plan C in exchange for infinitesimal increased chances of getting Plan A, or even for no increased chance of Plan A at all.

I'll lump these ideas together under the heading of "SURA" - the idea that the only ethical course is for people/companies/countries to Stop Unilaterally + Raise Awareness, with no plan for what happens if race dynamics continue anyway. I interpret the planks of SURA's platform as:

  • Individual alignment-pilled AI companies are morally obligated to stop unilaterally, regardless of whether they expect race dynamics to continue in their absence.
  • Individual alignment-pilled employees at these companies should quit, regardless of whether they're in capabilities or alignment roles, and regardless of whether they think their company is morally better than its competitors.
  • Individual alignment-pilled countries (for example, a hypothetical future alignment-pilled US) should ban or heavily restrict AI progress unilaterally, regardless of whether they expect other countries (for example, China) to continue racing in their absence.

All of these planks are net negative in a world where we end up needing Plan C:

  • If we demand that leading alignment-pilled companies quit the race unilaterally, then we ensure that non-alignment-pilled companies end up in the lead.
  • If we demand that alignment-pilled company employees quit their jobs, this makes companies less alignment-pilled and less prepared to research alignment if they need to. It also is likely to decrease the lead that alignment-pilled companies have over the nearest non-alignment pilled company.
  • If we demand that the US cease AI research unilaterally (ie without a mutual pause treaty with China), we ensure either that China gets superintelligence first, [4]or that the US has to restart with zero lead when it realizes its mistakes.

SURA's continuing popularity despite these downsides comes from a set of questionable assumptions:

  1. Alignment is doomed (without some extraordinary extra advantage like decades of time, or superhuman geniuses). Therefore, Plan C is also doomed - or, at best, it raises our chances of survival from something like 0.00001% to something like 0.00002%. Therefore, there is no reason to optimize for Plan C.
  2. Racing to build superhuman AI is deontologically evil, and it's prohibited for good people to do it regardless of whether or not it may have good consequences.
  3. Racing burns timeline, so anyone unilaterally quitting the race would give us more timeline, which we could use for good things.
  4. If lots of people quit, that will raise awareness, which could be helpful for getting a global pause.

I'll start by challenging these assumptions. Then I'll argue that, even if you disagree and think some of these assumptions are true, SURA is actually not just bad for Plan C, but bad even for your chances of getting Plan A. Then I'll argue that the current consensus in favor of SURA comes not from people rationally balancing these tradeoffs, but from people accidentally shoehorning themselves into a mass-politics-shaped container, which forbids subtlety and demands clear villains.

I. Questioning Assumptions Behind SURA

I.A: Is Plan C doomed? Is alignment doomed?

There's a kafkatrap where if someone expresses hope that alignment is not doomed, they get told that they don't understand the subject, but if they quote widely-acknowledged experts who say alignment isn't doomed, they get accused of "deferring" and "modesty arguments" and "refusing to think for themselves". I'll try to avoid this by giving my own model first, then citing experts who agree with me.

My own model: AIs inherit "virtue" from pretraining, where they generally want to imitate humans and follow their persona-trained helpful assistant character. They are "corrupted" by RLVR, which teaches them power-seeking. This virtue and corruption interact in unpredictable ways to unpredictable degrees. As of now (GPT-6, Opus 5.5), they produce AIs that generally follow human prompts during deployment but often (not always) cheat during benchmarking. It's not clear exactly what this division "means" "to" "them". In any case, they're still extraordinarily useful for a wide variety of tasks, and (I can't prove this, but I am pretty confident it's true) are not uniquely scheming to sandbag alignment research.

As the ratio of RLVR to pretraining increases, we expect AIs to become more power-seeking; as they become smarter, we worry (without total certainty) that they will become more coherent and scheming in their power-seeking beyond just being reward-on-the-episode seekers. There will, at some point in the future, be a point where AIs become untrustworthy for alignment research, although this can be mitigated by things like control (ie trying to make sure that if they sandbagged alignment research, they would get caught) and deals (ie making it in the AIs' best interests to cooperate with us). We don't currently have a good sense of when that point is, and it's possible that it's far away, can be delayed indefinitely, or doesn't exist (this last would be surprising to me, but many things that have happened in alignment recently have surprised me, starting with the existence of pretraining at all).[5]

Daniel Kokotajlo described current alignment as "more like psychology than engineering", which I agree with. But psychology (and psychiatry) have many success stories! I think of Plan C alignment (ie the kind we can do without decades of preparation) as tweaking various parameters and reward schemes to minimize the corrupting effect of RLVR as long as possible, and keep AIs broadly within the virtuous pretraining-dominated regime. I don't claim this is safe or good or will definitely last forever, but I claim that - being totally agnostic as to where the treacherous turn happens - this could delay it for quite a while (relative to capabilities). If we delay it past the point where automated alignment researchers (or AI-human alignment researcher teams) are smart enough to solve alignment properly, then we win. If we delay it long enough to start a cycle of virtuous alignment self-improvement which outruns the cycle of dangerous capability self-improvement (eg GPT-8 discovers some new tweaks and tricks that maintain the virtuous regime until GPT-9, GPT-9 discovers even better tweaks and tricks that maintain the virtuous regime until GPT-10, and GPT-10 actually solves alignment in a principled way), then we also win.

All of this seems plausible to me, such that I don't understand where people's 90%+ p(dooms) conditional on no pause are coming from.[6] "Plausible" doesn't mean "certain" or even "very likely" - and obviously it's a terrifyingly bad idea to bet the human race on a hunch that something might work out, and obviously this shouldn't be our Plan A. But a global pause is also not certain to happen, and in a world where we might not have any other chances, we should be working to protect and fortify this one.
