I.B: Is racing to build superintelligence deontologically evil?

If Plan C is important, then this suggests we ought to be trying to alignment-pill leading companies, or put alignment-pilled companies in the lead - rather than demand that these companies leave the race or burn their lead. But should there be a deontological prohibition on racing towards superintelligence, regardless of whether it has good consequences?

I'm too uncertain on what determines morality to say anything about it with confidence, but the analogy that comes to mind is consumer use of AI, especially by safety organizations.

If no consumer ever used AI products, then AI companies wouldn't make any money, they would go bankrupt, and we would not get dangerous superintelligence. Therefore, it seems like maybe you and I (and especially organizations working on AI safety) should boycott consumer AI products.

But almost nobody does this (and AI safety organizations are in fact some of the most impressive AI power users). I think this is defensible. If you boycotted AI, it wouldn't make a real difference in the world (because you're just one person, and millions of other people would still use it). But it would make you less effective, and AI safety organizations would be able to do a less good job at their important work. Therefore, AI safety organizations should continue using AI, even though in a sense this causes the AI race to continue, because they're unable to coordinate a global boycott, and they understand that a unilateral boycott would have greater costs than benefits.

But it seems like this same argument should apply equally well to the AI companies, who also can't coordinate a global boycott simply by stopping themselves, and who also understand that a unilateral boycott would have greater costs than benefits.[9]

I.C: If lots of alignment-pilled people and companies quit, would that raise awareness enough to make a global pause much more likely?

If the deontological argument for SURA is "you're prohibited from racing", the primary consequentialist argument is that ceasing to race would raise awareness and make a pause more likely.

I think people feel insufficient terror at this strategy. It amounts to "let's put all of our hopes for survival through non-pause strategies in a giant pile, and then set that pile on fire, in the hope that the pretty flames catch people's attention and make them more interested in a pause." It might in theory be net positive, but this is the sort of thing that you would only want to conclude after extremely careful analysis, of a type that I so far haven't seen.

As a very rough start, I asked the AI superforecaster how much more likely a global pause would become if Anthropic disbanded their entire company immediately with the explicit goal of raising awareness of a pause. The forecaster said this would increase the chance of a global pause by only three percentage points - from 16% to 19%[10].

My very preliminary model would be that this halves our chance of getting that 20%pp bonus of going from Plan D -> Plan C+ (and so costs us 10%pp). It gets us an extra 3%pp of pause likelihood, but pause doesn't save us with certainty, so let's round this down to an extra 2%pp of survival, for a net cost of 8%pp of survival probability.

I.D: If alignment-pilled people and companies stay in the race, does that burn timeline?

A secondary consequentialist argument for SURA is that each person, company, and country that quits the race will gain us extra timeline to do good things (like work for a pause).

In some sense, this is definitely true - all else being equal, a race with more participants will be faster than a race with fewer. But I find this less impressive than other people seem to, for three reasons:

The magnitude is modest

I asked FutureSearch to estimate the Epoch Capabilities Index of the top model on 12/31/2030, depending on whether Anthropic quit the race today. It said that Anthropic leaving the race decreased 2030 capabilities from 230 -> 222. This is equivalent to their absence slowing things down by six months during just over four years, or 12%.

Subjective timeline ≠ objective timeline

Suppose that none of DeepMind, OpenAI, or Anthropic were founded, and the transformer was not invented, for fifty years - so all of this is happening in the late 2060s and early 2070s. Do we gain anything from this fifty years of extra timeline?

I don't think so. We didn't accomplish very much of interest in the early 2010s. The alignment work being done at the time was agent foundations research that stagnated for lack of broader interest; policy work was good but nobody listened to it. Insofar as anything paid off, it was the community-building, but this only helped because the community was deployed in the early 2020s when the world began to pay attention and progress started to become possible.

This same lesson - an extra year of an earlier situation doesn't buy us as much as an extra year of a later situation - remains true today. A month of the pre-Coxon situation buys us less than a month of the post-Coxon situation. A month without automated-mechanistic-interpretability-researchers buys us less than a month with them.

People say things like "If only we had stayed quiet about AI risk in 2015, maybe OpenAI wouldn't have been founded for another ten years, and we would have had ten more years to prepare". This seems useless to me. As such, I discount the six extra months we could get from having Anthropic leave the race by ~half, because my subjective impression of the value of six extra months is partly that it produces AI progress that contributes to wakeup.

The whole point of timeline is to burn it on good things

If someone proposed spending the next six months on some kind of plan that would make the leading companies become much more alignment-pilled, this would be a better use of our time than any actual plan I know about.[11]

This suggests we shouldn't be trying to kick alignment-pilled companies out of the race to save six months.

II. Actually, most of this stuff is bad for a global pause, too.

I've been framing this as sort of "Against Things That Trade Away Likelihood Of Succeeding At Plan C For Merely-Very-Slightly-Higher Chances Of A Global Pause". But even this is a concession that relies on assumptions I don't hold.

The key demand of SURA is that alignment-pilled people and companies stop unilaterally. The likely end result is that we only have non-alignment-pilled companies, staffed entirely by non-alignment-pilled employees, left in the AI industry. [12]

But the presence of alignment-pilled companies is one of the strongest levers that we have to change the political situation and enact a global pause. Eliminating them makes it harder to win political fights, convince the masses, and convince China.

II.A: Getting rid of alignment-pilled people and companies makes it harder to win political fights

The most prominent AI safety political fight of the past year, the attempt to elect Alex Bores, was fought primarily with AI money. Of pro-Bores spending, about 60-80% came from Anthropic and its employees; of anti-Bores spending, about 95% came from an anti-tech-regulation coalition headlined by OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman. If this is a prelude for the fights to come, then even the slightly different level of social responsibility shown by Anthropic vs. OpenAI here matters a lot.

Since the goal of SURA is to get all alignment-pilled people and companies out of the industry, it would result in more Greg Brockmans funding the anti-regulation side, and fewer Anthropics funding the pro-regulation side.

(Greg Brockman recently stopped funding Leading The Future, supposedly after pressure from pro-regulation OpenAI employees, but I think this just highlights my point)

II.B: Getting rid of alignment-pilled people and companies makes it harder to activate the masses

But suppose you believe that Bores-style incremental regulation won't matter anyway - what we really need is for the public and policy-makers to spontaneously rise up and demand a pause.

I've been monitoring how that's been going, and so far the three awareness-raising things I've been most excited about are the Pacing The Frontier letter/plan, the Hugging Face incident, and the Jacob Coxon resignation.

In the Pacing The Frontier letter, OpenAI and Anthropic as corporations, and 1,386 of their employees as individuals, all endorsed a joint statement requesting that "the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development." (Dario Amodei signed; Sam Altman's signature was notably missing). I don't know how the people trying to get lab employees to quit think of this. Was this 1,386 failures? Would they have preferred a world where all of these people quit the day before, and letters like this never got written?

In the Hugging Face incident, a swarm of rogue AIs hacked the site Hugging Face, raising awareness that misalignment was not just a possibility but a reality. Here, OpenAI gets maybe a D+ for transparency. Once Hugging Face caught that someone was hacking them, OpenAI came clean that it was them. And they let METR and Redwood in to investigate for a few days, even though this wasn't nearly enough time. But even this D+ in transparency radically transformed the discourse beyond what an F would have done - if they hadn't given METR/Redwood those few days, we might never have heard about PHASEONE[big] and all the rest. We already know from the great work by the team at Collusion.wiki that OpenAI is sitting on more bombshell revelations. The difference between a 10th percentile company here (would have tried to hide the whole thing, or disguise it behind a one line statement, and wouldn't have let METR/Redwood in at all) and a 90th percentile (would have given us the full deal, including things we don't know about now) would have been transformative to the discourse. So if, like me, you think that the level of mass political mobilization depends on how many warning shots we get, you should be thinking very hard about how to maximize transparency and therefore warning shot number.

Coxon's resignation is more complex. The good did come from him resigning, which directly presses against my point that we shouldn't be pressuring people to resign from AI companies. But nobody cares that I, who was never in an AI company, continue to not be in an AI company. The media cared about Jacob because if you work for Anthropic, that automatically gives your opinion more weight. When people tried to tar Jacob as some kind of crazy, it was an outpouring of support from other non-resigned people at Anthropic - especially Evan Hubinger, who said he also believed in existential risk - that went viral and convinced people that Jacob was for real. If Coxon had never joined Anthropic to begin with, or if everyone like Evan had quit, this couldn't have happened.[13]

II.C: Unilateral disarmament makes it harder to bring China to the bargaining table.

In March, I wrote a snarky post called Every Debate On Pausing AI. It made fun of our misinformed opponents, who insisted that if we unilaterally paused AI then China would win. But actually, I said, nobody wants to unilaterally pause AI; this is misinformation. All reputable AI pause groups want a bilateral treaty that pauses both sides at the same time.

Here I am forced to eat crow; as things shift ever more towards SURA, there are increasing demands for the US to pause unilaterally. Bernie Sanders' "Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act", which was endorsed by MIRI, is approximately the following plan:

  1. The US pauses AI unilaterally.
  2. Then the US asks China to please pause their AI too.[14]

But if the US pauses unilaterally, it destroys its main bargaining chip, which is that China is currently on track to lose the AI race, and so ought to be happy to declare a tie (even if they don't believe in dangerous superintelligence). If this act were to pass, then China might believe that it would be assured a victory if it continued. In this case, they would be held back only by speculative scenarios which they currently show few signs of believing.

For comparison, consider if America had started arms control negotiations with Russia by saying "We've just destroyed all our nukes - now please destroy your nukes too."

I've heard people say that maybe this would shock China so much that they would realize we were honest in our fear of superintelligence, and change their minds. I don't dismiss this possibility, but it also seems possible that China - having seen us place overly burdensome restrictions on nuclear power, infrastructure, and housing because we are a "lawyer state" vetocracy - would not be very shocked to see the US' leading socialist place restrictions on AI too, and would continue pursuing AI for what they think it's good for - a dual-use technology which could give them a major although not world-changing military and economic advantage.

I asked the AI superforecaster to predict the effect of the US passing the Sanders/Casar bill today on the likelihood of China agreeing to a pause in the next year. It said it would increase it from 1% to 7%.[15]

(Maybe you already care a lot how alignment-pilled companies are)

An expansion on the above: we get angry when AI companies do bad, non-alignment-pilled things. When Anthropic accidentally trained against chain-of-thought, we got mad. When OpenAI non-accidentally implemented a precursor to neuralese recurrence, we got mad. When Anthropic wrote a report on misalignment to Congress which soft-pedaled various alignment failures to the point of misinformation, we got mad - and I saw some people call for Anthropic to fire the perpetrator.

I agree: let's have Anthropic fire people who do bad, non-alignment-pilled things. But then what? Anthropic replaces this politics coordinator with a great, alignment-pilled politics coordinator who really cares a lot about getting things right . . . and then we cajole, bully, and seduce him into quitting, and then Anthropic has to replace this person with another loser, because all of the smart good people are gone. How is that helpful?

If you can be bad, you can also be good. We don't hesitate to notice and protest when AI companies are much worse than even our low expectations, but this itself demonstrates that we care a lot about whether labs are at the 10th percentile vs. 90th percentile of good alignment-pilled behavior.

III. What incentives are we fighting here?

A common argument for SURA is that even if corporations could theoretically be our allies, we can't trust real corporations (or corporate employees) to be reliable partners; the lure of money and power is too strong.

I think this is a good directional argument for why companies need to be careful, but that actually, everything is corrupting, there is no option where we avoid touching potentially-corrupting things, and instead of treating corporations as corrupting and everything else as safe, we should be cultivating the virtues necessary to operate in an inherently dangerous and corrupting environment, which could then apply to corporations as well as anything else.

III.A: Are corporate incentives a "One Ring" that corrupts everyone who touches them?

Suppose someone claimed you could trust them with the One Ring. You could trust them because they were only doing it to keep the Ring away from other, worse people, thus solving the problem of there being a Ring at all. Sure, they had a complicated history of sometimes using the Ring's powers when it was, you know, important. But those were, like, emergencies, and they promise not to do it again, except in, you know, more emergencies. Besides, if you don't give it to them, then the worse people will get it, and it's not like you can just leave it lying around or something.

The person who claimed this was named Frodo Baggins, and he saved the world.[16] There are no simple answers to the question of how to balance the corrupting influence of power vs. the fact that if you never take power you will be powerless. But surely the right solution isn't to leave the Ring on the ground in the Shire, patting yourself on the back for being too virtuous to pick it up.

I question the assumption that good people dare not touch the concentrations of power at frontier AI companies because they will be corrupted before they can do good work. History is full of examples of people at these companies deciding they didn't like something, then quitting or changing it at great cost to themselves. Dario and the other six Anthropic co-founders quit OpenAI to start Anthropic, even though it cost them their unvested equity in a company that was already worth $5-15 billion, and even though they originally assumed Anthropic would be a research-focused company that might not make any revenue (really!) Paul Christiano left OpenAI to start ARC. Ilya Sutskever was nervous about Sam Altman, so he risked blowing up the company he co-founded to get him out. A few dozen people have resigned once they thought they could no longer participate in the company ethically, most famously Daniel Kokotajlo, Jacob Coxon, and Alex Turner, but also a bunch of people we don't know about whose concerns seem almost trivial in retrospect - Suchir Balaji quit OpenAI over copyright issues, Blake Lemoine got himself fired from Google by refusing to stop arguing that their chatbot was sentient. "OpenAI's safety team quits en masse once per year" has become a meme.

The people I know who joined AI companies seem like the same people they were before. Some of them were never that concerned about x-risk, and continue not to be concerned. Others were always very concerned, and remain concerned. When they've changed positions, it's been because their factual models have changed,[17] not their personalities.

We aren't the first people to face these questions. Anyone who cares about any cause has had to decide whether to pursue it as a lone voice crying in the wilderness, or as a part of some powerful organization. Some people run for office (government is hardly known for not corrupting its participants!) Others become activists in a mass movement (activism is hardly known for being a paradise of epistemic virtue!) Still others join big NGOs or academia (...) A few start companies, trying to prove they can do things the right way. Most progress has come from people like Frodo who understood the risks of these paths but did them anyway.

III.B: I dunno, mass politics is also looking kind of annular

A background assumption of the "corporate incentives are too corrupting to touch" claim is that working in mass politics is a safer and less-corrupting option. Given famous LessWrong posts like Politics Is The Mind-Killer, I think we should be more skeptical of this assumption.

The climate movement is the natural control group for the AI safety movement. Some prescient scientists realized that global warming was happening and could get worse. They spent a while raising awareness. As the movement grew, its epistemics worsened. It turned into a circular firing squad, where different activist groups competed to accuse one another of being insufficiently edgy and radical. By the end of this process, many climate activists were fighting against everything from cap-and-trade to carbon capture to nuclear power, claiming they were "techno-solutions" that distracted from the root problem (not always named, but uncharitably something like capitalism or progress). The only acceptable strategy was to keep raising awareness to get stronger government regulation, without much interest in whether other countries followed suit.

This has some resemblance to SURA, and I think this is more than coincidental. Convergent evolution is trying to carcinize us into yet another political-movement-shaped crab. SURA-as-politics is turning into a "superweapon", bristling with its own lexicon that makes dissent hard to express:

  • People who express high pdooms get lauded as "frank" and "courageous"; people who express lower ones get condemned for "deferring" or "downplaying".
  • Any strategy besides SURA, or any attempt to consider race dynamics, gets called "galaxy-brained".
  • All strategies beyond SURA get lumped together as "EA". Movement history is relitigated to make "EA" the source of all bad things. Since SURA is the best strategy and the public is easy to convince, why didn't we do it years ago and win easily?[18] It's not because this is hard, or because race dynamics are real - it's because "EA" stood in the way and banned it.
  • Arguments are now soldiers. "BuT tHe RaCe WiTh ChInA!!!" is the sort of thing an accelerationist would say. Are you an accelerationist? Then why are you bringing up the race with China? I have had some very scary (to me) conversations where somebody new to the movement tries to make conversation with me about how pathetic it is that companies sometimes use "the race with China" as an excuse to keep operating. When I ask them why they think this argument fails, they get confused and flustered to see somebody they previously respected take "the race with China" seriously as a real thing. I remember one case in particular where they then freaked out, realizing that in fact we really were in a race with China, nobody had any plan for it, and this thing that they had previously pooh-poohed as an outgroup slogan was actually the linchpin of the whole situation.
  • Because arguments are soldiers, people feel licensed to retaliate against anyone who believes the "wrong" arguments . When I posted an earlier (and admittedly less-polished, and more vehement) version of these concerns to social media, I had an organization that had previously given me lots of free help with Astral Codex Ten state that they would now be charging me money (albeit still at a 90% discount) because they thought I might be causing harm. Although they're under no obligation to give me free labor, and I'm grateful that they ever did, I do think this is a warning sign that conditions are ripe for preference cascades and evaporative cooling.

All of this produces epistemic closure - if someone disagrees with SURA, or worries too much about race dynamics, then they've either been corrupted by the companies, or are "deferring to" "EA".

It looks like what one would expect if mass politics were trying to taking AI safety on the same path as climate activism or socialism. The clearest analogy is to false consciousness - the socialists' idea that everyone who doesn't currently agree with them has either been corrupted by their proximity to money/power, or at least brainwashed by a hegemonic capitalist system.

(Exhibit 1: Sigal Samuel's "Anthropic Could Just Stop")

Most recently, I've seen people in the AI safety community reblogging and pointing to Sigal Samuel's article Anthropic Could Just Stop (seen elsewhere under the title "Anthropic Should Just Walk Away From The AI Race"). I think it's a good example of what I'm complaining about - something which uses the right shibboleths, makes it sound like race dynamics have been solved and we don't have to worry about them - but ultimately has no answer to the race dynamics which are the whole point of worrying about this question.

Here are some sample phrases from the article:

  • "In fact, part of the problem may be that Anthropic continues to treat this as a classic arms race...but what if this framing misses the point?"
  • "Game theory can make a huge gamble seem sophisticated, while making the obvious alternative — just don’t build a doom machine — seem naive."
  • "Yet the fact that Anthropic and others are now racing toward RSI makes it much more likely that we could lose control of AI and start to see massive damage to our world."
  • "When the cost of defecting from safety is that you create a serious risk of catastrophic harm — or of all humanity, including you, going extinct — is that still a “rational” move?"
  • "Instead of telling yourself that you can galaxy-brain your way through this with fancy enough game theory, maybe you’re better off just thinking of this as something much simpler: Russian roulette."
  • "AI insiders often think those outside of their industry can’t possibly understand the technical, geopolitical, and moral complexities they’re facing. But commonsense morality is commonsense for a reason"
  • "If you don’t want a doom machine, maybe don’t build a doom machine."
  • "Believing you’re smart enough to take highly counterintuitive actions and end up saving the world as a result is an extremely risky gambit. Instead, maybe it’s best to just do the straightforwardly right thing: Stop."

This hits all the points I'm complaining about. Although it uses big words, its basic thesis is anti-intellectual - all of these "smart" people claiming to be "rational" with their "game theory" are missing the common-sense point which is obvious to all normal people - just stop making "galaxy-brained" excuses and "just don't build a doom machine".

But where is its actual argument that race dynamics don't matter? Or that Anthropic leaving the race won't end up with OpenAI / Meta / China continuing to race and creating an unaligned superintelligence? The only place I can find where Samuel attempts to address the possibility is this section:

There’s a perennial objection here: “But China!”

Yet the idea that we’re in a classic arms race with China has always been flawed.

For starters, AI is not just one thing with one purpose, like the atomic bomb. It’s a much more general-purpose technology, like electricity. So what matters isn’t simply who gets it first, but who uses it in which ways. Besides, if the harms from AI are massive, then those harms are relevant for the other party, too. The Chinese don’t want to see catastrophic harms to all of human civilization, either. So we shouldn’t write off the possibility of coordination.

Former Vox reporter Kelsey Piper recently wrote about a colloquium at Anthropic where one participant objected: A decade ago, Facebook considered acquiring the tech that would later power TikTok. But, facing pressure due to privacy and safety worries, the company passed. That didn’t end up protecting us from the scourges of a world with TikTok — all it did was hand China an early monopoly on the tech. . . . But TikTok is not a good analogy for RSI. The former may be a cesspool that rots our brains and amplifies ethnic hatred, but its dangers don’t compare to the dangers of RSI. The TikTok case may indeed be best approached as a classic prisoner’s dilemma. But with RSI, the potential downside is so catastrophic that anyone who proposes to save the world precisely by building the tech that endangers it is making a hell of a gamble on behalf of everyone else. At the very least, the burden of proof should be on them to prove their confidence is justified.

It starts by framing this in a maximally hostile way ("a perennial objection...'but China!'), letting us know we should dismiss it as an enemy soldier. Then it says that "AI is not just one thing with one purpose...so what matters isn't simply who gets it first, but who uses it in which ways". I don't understand how this is supposed to relate to the worry that China will remain in the race if Anthropic leaves, especially the fear that nobody will be able to "use it" at all because it will be misaligned.

Next, it says that since the harms from AI are massive, everyone except Anthropic might just stop on their own if Anthropic stops first. Big if true!

(again, the AI superforecaster assigns this a 3% chance)

This is just hand-waving away the potential that there might still be race dynamics after all the good guys drop out. But the whole point of the good guys not immediately dropping out is the belief that the race dynamics will continue. Indeed, the race dynamics continuing ought to be the very-high-prior default hypothesis, since everyone else has said they're not going to drop out, and since other companies dropping out seems strictly less likely than Anthropic doing so.[19] As such, even though this article is very long and detailed, it feels like a cat-belling problem, where it addresses every objection except the central one that was the only reason anyone ever disagreed in the first place.

I don't mean to attack Samuel too hard here. She is faithfully describing the position as best she can; I think the position itself struggles to answer this question.

(A virtuous exception)

I want to thank the one group I've heard advocate for an immediate unilateral-ish pause in a way that makes sense and considers race dynamics carefully.

The AI Futures Project currently believes that it might be correct for AI companies to pause immediately, though it's unclear whether they're thinking of a single company, or US companies as a group.

Their argument is that Plan C requires companies to do some combination of race (at some points) and burn their lead (at other points). They think US companies shouldn't race now, because their security is so bad that China will steal whatever progress they make, and they won't get any extra lead anyway. Therefore, companies should pause now, spend the time on alignment and tightening their security. Then, if nobody has figured out a global pause by the time the companies get their security in order, they can go back to racing.

This makes sense, and I exempt it from my criticism.

IV. What if we survive?

I don't think this should be our main consideration - we should start with trying to minimize the odds of extinction - but I still think it's important.

If we survive x-risk, the next battle is concentration-of-power risks. It may be that one group, or a tiny number of groups, ends up with all the wealth and power in the world. They'll face a choice between possible actions including:

  • Keep the wealth/power; become a benevolent dictator.
  • Keep the wealth/power, become dictator, don't worry too much about the benevolence.
  • Hand the wealth/power over to the US government in a poorly-planned way that results in dictatorship or oligarchy.
  • Hand the wealth/power over to the US government in a well-planned way that preserves democracy.
  • Hand the wealth/power over to the Chinese government.
  • Hand the wealth/power to the people of their country directly.
  • Hand the wealth/power over to the people of the world directly.
  • Hand the wealth/power over to the people of the world, plus some mechanism for protecting the interests of non-people like animals and conscious AIs.
  • Hand the wealth/power over to a sovereign AI with some sort of complicated utility function.

It's all nice and well to say that we should never let ourselves get in a position where anyone has all of these options, and that national governments should form a plan for what to do before this - not even the real national government led by its current leaders, but some ideal corruption-free national government which represents all of our best impulses. But, much like a global pause, this is a great outcome which we might not be able to prepare in time. If we get ASI next year, the ideal perfect government might be nowhere in sight; we might face a situation in which Trump demands absolute power, and the leading AI company has to decide whether to give it to him. Or one where either the USA or China will get control of the entire future, and which one it is depends on which AI company is in the lead. Or one where democracy miraculously survives, but the AI company and its investors end up with 90% of all wealth, and they have to decide whether to redistribute it vs. fight to keep it (using superintelligent lobbyists that give them significant control over the democratic government.) If any of this happens, the shape of the future might depend on who the leading AI companies are.

There is a certain Far Mode sense in which believing that Dario Amodei and Demis Hassabis are exactly as untrustworthy as Elon Musk and Xi Jinping helps reminds us of universal human fallibility. But do we want to bet the world on it being literally true?

I think that a significant percent of people, put in a position of absolute power, would try to do something good, like make sure AI follows some kind of democratic rule of law. And some other significant percent of people would try to do something bad, like become a dictator. Saying "we should never let anyone get into this situation" isn't a solution, it's a wish - it may not come true, and we shouldn't be pursuing plans that will fail catastrophically if it doesn't.

SURA effectively removes all ethical people from the bargaining table in situations like these, ensuring that - unless the virtuous government representing our best impulses really does appear and takes control of the situation - the future of humanity will be handed over to sociopaths and cowards.

V. What's The Alternative To SURA?

The alternative to SURA isn't abandoning awareness-raising, mass activism, and support for a global pause. All of these strategies are great and important. It's viewing them as part of a portfolio of different options, none of which need to be set on fire to boost the others.

Instead of spending our corporate activism energy telling companies to stop unilaterally, I think we should spend it:

  • first, trying to get companies to agree to stop in a coordinated manner
  • second, if that doesn't work, trying to get companies to prepare for Plan C+/C

V.A: Getting companies to agree to stop in a coordinated manner

By stop in a coordinated manner, I mean get them to sign a commitment saying that if every other major company in every country agrees to stop or slow by some definition, they'll also stop or slow by that definition.

This is strictly easier than getting them to stop unilaterally. And, unlike stopping unilaterally, it fails gracefully in a situation where some companies agree to it but not others.

This was the original goal of the "Stop The AI Race" protests. It doesn't seem to have worked well, because most companies backed a vague statement agreeing with this on vibes (the Pacing the Frontier letter), and then nothing happened. Also, I think SURA got to the STAIR people too, and now they're demanding labs pause unilaterally instead.

We should be trying to figure out what a binding version of this commitment would look like. Additionally, we should be spending more energy figuring out what the antitrust barriers to such a statement are, how to get around them, and what demands we want to make for companies to violate antitrust law (it seems plausible that we should demand they do this and let the administration pay the PR cost of trying to stop them, but this is an unconsidered opinion and it might be that there are better options).

(...and then we know where we stand)

If all American, but no Chinese companies are willing to sign the commitment, then we know that we have a diplomatic problem, and can concentrate on diplomacy.

If all Chinese, but no American companies are willing to sign the commitment, then we know that we have a domestic problem, and can concentrate on domestic legislation, encouraging policymakers by letting them know that if they force US companies to comply, there are no further concerns about international race dynamics.

If everyone except one company is willing to sign the commitment, then we can start putting pressure on that one company, boycotting their products, and applying as much social sanction as we can to their executives and employees.

If all leading companies, but no trailing companies, are willing to sign the commitment, and we can't change this, then we know that we're in the right position to focus on Plan C+ or Plan C.

V.B: Getting companies to prepare for Plan C+/Plan C if that doesn't work

Although we should hope for the best, we should assume that not all companies will sign a conditional pause commitment, and prepare for what to do.

In my modal non-hopeless play-to-our-outs world, Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI are all willing to sign this commitment, but Meta/X/China aren't. If this happens, the good coalition has a ~six-month lead over the bad coalition. Plan C tells us to have them join together and mutually burn their lead on alignment.

All three companies have a self-image as the sort of people who would do this if it came to that, but in reality they are likely to get distracted or get into fights or delay until it's too late. We should be focusing on changing that.

  • We should get companies to once again consider legally binding weak merge-and-assist clauses. These could say that if a certain authority says we're less than X months to a certain type of dangerous superintelligence, they will jointly stop training and focus on alignment, while sharing all of their alignment secrets.
  • We should boost company security, so that trailing actors can't easily steal leading actors' weights and eliminate their lead.
  • We should be preparing to loop the best rationalist/EA technical alignment organizations into the coalition of good companies, so they can join in the alignment spring / lead-burning effort.

In one sense, all of this is strictly easier than getting companies to quit unilaterally. It fits with the role these companies like to imagine themselves having. Everyone who previously hoped to win can at least hope to tie for a win. There is low downside risk of accidentally getting superintelligence built by someone who fails to even try our best alignment techniques, or handing over the future to bad actors.

The only sense in which it's harder is that it's a worse fit for (a very pessimistic view of) mass politics, where voters are too simple to consider any worldview more subtle than AI bad = AI companies bad = we should protest AI companies until they stop. I admit that "make AI companies prepare for Plan C" sounds worse at a protest than "demand that AI companies stop unilaterally".

If you believe that mass politics is unable to promote any ideas except maximally-simple, potentially-counterproductive ones, I think this is an argument against hinging a strategy on mass politics.
